0.name: block
0.value:
Finds the smallest value in an array - in the whole array, or in each row or each column.

Use it for the trough of a signal, the quietest channel, the closest of a set of distances, or the darkest pixel of an image. To know WHERE the smallest value is rather than what it is, use np.argmin.

NOT THE SAME AS np.min:
np.amin REDUCES - an array goes in and one value (or one per row or column) comes out. np.min, a different node, works element by element: it compares every value with a fixed number and keeps the smaller, so an array goes in and an array of the same shape comes out (a ceiling). np.min is the clamp; np.amin is the question "what is the smallest?".

THE axis MENU:
None reduces the WHOLE array to one answer. 0 reduces down each COLUMN (across the rows), giving one answer per column. 1 reduces along each ROW (across the columns), giving one answer per row. In general the axis you name is the one that disappears: an 8 by 10 array reduced along axis 0 gives 10 answers, along axis 1 gives 8. The answers come out as a flat 1-D array - the reduced axis is removed, not kept as a length-1 axis (there is no keepdims option).

SYNTAX:
np.amin <axis: int>
Default: no axis - the whole array.

EXAMPLE:
np.amin 0

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

in:
The array. Every array that arrives is reduced and the answer sent;
this is the only inlet that makes the node send.
A list is turned into an array. A single number is sent back as itself while axis is None (with an axis set, it sends nothing). An empty array is an error and nothing is sent.
If the array holds a NaN (not-a-number) the answer is NaN - there is no nan-skipping version of this node.

axis (menu, also an inlet):
None, or one of the input's axes. A number typed after the node name sets it (np.amin 1); with no number it starts at None. The menu lists None, 0 and 1 at first, and once an array arrives it lists None and exactly that array's axes (0, 1, 2 for a 3-D array). If the chosen axis is past the end of a smaller array, that array is reduced along its last axis, but the choice is kept for the arrays that follow. Changing the axis does NOT send by itself; the next array uses it. Pick None in the menu, or send the message None into the axis inlet, to reduce the whole array again.

OUTPUTS:

amin:
With axis None, one number (the smallest value). With an axis, an array holding the smallest value of each row or column. It has the type of the input.

READING THE DEMO:
make_dark_spot draws 8 by 10 of light noise (0.4 to 1) with one dark cell, exactly 0, where the two sliders put it (load_bang starts it at row 5, column 6). np.amin with axis None, top right, always answers 0: the spot is the smallest value wherever it is. np.amin 1 asks each ROW: its 8 answers stand in the column beside the picture, each next to its row (np.expand_dims only stands the flat row of 8 up as a column), and the spot's row reads 0. np.amin 0 asks each COLUMN: the strip under the picture has 10 answers, one under each column, and the spot's column reads 0. Move a slider and the 0 moves with the spot.

RELATED:
np.amax finds the largest. np.argmin gives the position of the smallest. np.min is the element-wise ceiling described above, not a reduction. np.mean and np.median summarise the middle instead of the extremes. t.min is the PyTorch version.
